preamble: Palatalization and weakening of /ɡ/ to the palatal glide /j/, typically next to front vowels. It happened independently in Old English (Proto-West Germanic *gelu > ġeolu, Modern 'yellow'), in mainland North Germanic (Old Norse geit > Norwegian geit [jæɪt]), in Ibero-Romance (Latin rēgem > Spanish rey) and in Turkish (Old Anatolian Turkish beg > bey).

examples.note: Initial *g before front vowels became /j/ (spelled ġ in Old English, y in Modern English).
Old Norse /ɡ/ before front vowels became /j/ in Norwegian and Swedish; the spelling kept g.
Intervocalic g before a front vowel weakened to /j/; the final vowel was then lost.
Front-vowel g became the glide /j/ in syllable-final position.

⟨y⟩ = [j]. Kossmann's correspondence table gives Riffian y for Proto-Berber *g, distinct from the ʒ that continues *gʲ; Riffian shows the same words (ayeř, uyur, iyyar, yar, aryaz 'man'), but the Tarifit description records an intermediate [ʝ] still heard outside Central Tarifit (aɡ̠enduz [æʝəndʊz] beside ayenduz 'calf'), so Riffian is not counted as a one-step change here.
